title: The nuclear model of the atom
examTip: When describing Rutherford's experiment, link each observation to its conclusion. Most go straight through: the atom is mostly empty space. A few are deflected through large angles: the positive nucleus repels them. Very few bounce back: the nucleus is small and dense. Each observation needs its own explanation for full marks.
introTips: Scientists in the early 1900s didn't know atoms had a nucleus at all. They thought positive charge was spread evenly throughout.
Rutherford's experiment was one of the most surprising in physics. He said it was as shocking as firing a shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back.
The nuclear model we use today was built on Rutherford's work. It took decades to refine.
Proton number (atomic number) tells you the element. Mass number tells you the total number of protons and neutrons.
Electrons are at fixed energy levels. They move between levels when they absorb or emit electromagnetic radiation.
intro: How do you find out what is inside something you cannot see? That was the challenge facing physicists in the early 1900s. They fired tiny particles at atoms and watched where they went. This led to one of the most important discoveries in science: the nucleus. This story is not just history. It shows how evidence forces scientists to drop a comfortable model and replace it with a better one. The nuclear model it produced is still used today.

keyPoints.heading: Thomson's plum pudding model
keyPoints.content: Before the electron was discovered, scientists thought atoms were tiny spheres that could not be divided. Then J.J. Thomson discovered the electron (1897). This is a tiny, negatively charged particle. Its discovery led to Thomson's plum pudding model (1904). The model said the atom was a sphere of diffuse positive charge, with electrons embedded throughout it. It was like plums in a pudding. The atom was neutral overall, because the negative electrons balanced the spread-out positive charge. This model predicted what would happen if you fired particles at atoms. They would all pass straight through, with very slight deflections. The positive charge was too spread out to cause big deflections. Most particles did pass straight through. But a few were deflected through large angles, and some bounced back. The model could not explain this. That is what made Rutherford's results so dramatic.
writeBullets: Before the electron was discovered, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided
Thomson's plum pudding model — the atom is a sphere of diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded in it
Thomson discovered the electron in 1897. It is a tiny, negatively charged particle
The model predicted that fired particles would pass straight through, with only tiny deflections
The atom is neutral overall. The negative electrons balance the spread-out positive charge
The alpha particle scattering experiment disproved this model

keyTerms.def: Thomson's model: a sphere of diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding
A tiny, negatively charged particle in the atom; discovered by Thomson in 1897

keyPoints.memTip: Plum pudding = positive 'dough' with electron 'plums' dotted through it. It was replaced by Rutherford's nuclear model.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to contrast the plum pudding prediction (all particles go through) with what Rutherford really found.

keyPoints.heading: Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment
keyPoints.content: In 1909, Geiger and Marsden worked with Rutherford. They fired a beam of alpha particles at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. Alpha particles are positively charged and came from a radioactive source. A screen that flashed when hit showed where the particles went. This is called the alpha particle scattering experiment. There were three key observations, each with a conclusion. (1) Most alpha particles went straight through → the atom is mostly empty space. (2) A few alpha particles were deflected through large angles → the positive charge is not spread through the atom. The plum pudding model was wrong. The charge is packed into a small region at the centre. This region repels the alpha particles. (3) A very small number bounced almost straight back → there is an extremely small, dense nucleus. It holds the positive charge and most of the mass. Only alpha particles heading almost straight at the nucleus are pushed back. They are repelled before they reach it. This new evidence led to the nuclear model. It replaced the plum pudding model.
writeBullets: Alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil. A detector screen recorded where they went
Most went straight through → atom is mostly empty space
A few deflected through large angles → the positive charge is packed into a small region, which repels them
Very few bounced almost back → nucleus is tiny, dense and holds most of the mass
Result: the plum pudding model was dropped, and the nuclear model was proposed

keyTerms.def: Rutherford's 1909 experiment: alpha particles fired at thin gold foil; results showed atoms have a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
Atomic model proposed by Rutherford: tiny, dense, positive nucleus at the centre with electrons orbiting in empty space
A particle consisting of 2 protons + 2 neutrons; positively charged; used as the 'probe' in Rutherford's experiment

keyPoints.memTip: Most through = empty space. A few deflect a lot = small positive nucleus repels.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exam questions often ask 'what does observation X tell us about the structure of the atom?'. Link each result directly to a conclusion about structure.

keyPoints.heading: Structure of the atom — protons, neutrons and electrons
keyPoints.content: Atoms are very small. An atom has a radius of about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ metres. This number is in standard form. It means 0.0000000001 m. The nuclear model gives us the structure of the atom. There is a tiny, dense, positive nucleus at the centre. The radius of the nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of the radius of the atom. Most of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus. The nucleus is surrounded by negatively charged electrons. Almost all of the atom is empty space. The nucleus contains: - protons (positive charge, relative mass 1) - neutrons (no charge, relative mass 1) Electrons are outside the nucleus (relative charge −1, relative mass very small). Key numbers: - Atomic number (proton number, Z) = number of protons = number of electrons in a neutral atom. It decides the element. - Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons. - Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Example: carbon-12 has atomic number 6 → 6 protons, 6 electrons. Its mass number is 12 → 12 − 6 = 6 neutrons. In an atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. So an atom has no overall charge. An atom that loses one or more outer electrons becomes a positive ion. An ion is a charged particle. It forms when an atom loses or gains electrons. Its charge is written at the top right. A lithium atom that loses one electron is written Li⁺. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are both carbon, with 6 protons each. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8. You write an atom like this: ¹²₆C. The top number is the mass number. The bottom number is the atomic number. So ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C are isotopes: same bottom number, different top number.
writeBullets: Atom radius about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Nucleus radius less than 1/10 000 of the atom's radius
Nucleus — tiny, dense and positive. Contains protons and neutrons, and most of the mass
Proton — relative charge +1, relative mass 1
Neutron — relative charge 0, relative mass 1
Electron — relative charge −1, relative mass very small. Outside the nucleus
Atomic number (Z) = number of protons = number of electrons (neutral atom)
Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = A − Z
Isotopes — same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons
An atom that loses outer electrons becomes a positive ion, written with a + (for example Li⁺)

keyTerms.def: The number of protons in the nucleus; determines which element the atom is
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
A neutral particle in the nucleus; relative mass 1, relative charge 0
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons: same atomic number, different mass number
An atom that has lost one or more outer electrons, so it has an overall positive charge

keyPoints.memTip: A = protons + neutrons. Z = protons only.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise reading isotope notation like ²³⁸₉₂U. The top number is the mass number. The bottom is the atomic number.

keyPoints.heading: Energy levels and later changes to the model
keyPoints.content: Niels Bohr changed the nuclear model. He suggested that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. His calculations agreed with what experiments showed. Each distance matches a fixed energy level. Levels further from the nucleus are higher energy levels. When an electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation, it moves further from the nucleus, to a higher energy level. When it emits electromagnetic radiation, it moves closer to the nucleus, to a lower energy level. Later experiments showed that the positive charge of a nucleus is made of a whole number of smaller particles. Each one has the same positive charge. These particles were called protons. About 20 years after the nucleus was accepted, James Chadwick's experiments showed that the nucleus also holds neutrons. Each time new evidence was found, the model of the atom was changed.
writeBullets: Bohr: electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. His calculations agreed with experiments
Each distance matches a fixed energy level. Further out = higher energy level
Absorb electromagnetic radiation → the electron moves to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus
Emit electromagnetic radiation → the electron moves to a lower energy level, closer to the nucleus
Later experiments: the positive charge is made of protons. Chadwick showed the nucleus also holds neutrons

keyTerms.def: A fixed amount of energy an electron can have; each level is at a specific distance from the nucleus, and electrons move between levels by absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation

keyPoints.memTip: Absorb = move up a level, further out. Emit = move down a level, closer in.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Be able to say which way an electron moves. Absorbing electromagnetic radiation moves it to a higher energy level. Emitting radiation moves it to a lower one.

tables.title: Alpha particle scattering — observations and conclusions
rows: Most alpha particles passed straight through
A few alpha particles deflected through large angles
Positive charge is packed into a small region at the centre, which repels them
A very few bounced almost straight back
Nucleus is tiny, dense and contains most of the atom's mass

0.question: In Thomson's plum pudding model, where was the positive charge in an atom?
options: Spread evenly through a diffuse sphere, with electrons embedded in it
Concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus at the centre
Only in the electrons, which carried both positive and negative charges
In a ring around the outside of the atom
0.correctFeedback: Correct! In the plum pudding model, positive charge was spread through the atom like a pudding. Electrons ('plums') were dotted through it.
0.wrongFeedback: The plum pudding model pictured positive charge spread evenly through the whole atom, not in a central nucleus. The nucleus idea came later, from Rutherford's experiment.

1.question: In Rutherford's experiment, a very small number of alpha particles bounced almost straight back. What does this tell us?
options: The nucleus is very small and dense, with a large positive charge packed into it
The atom is mostly empty space with no charge
Alpha particles are negatively charged and attracted to the centre
The gold foil was too thick for most particles to pass through
1.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Only a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus could send an alpha particle back. A spread-out charge would not repel it that strongly.
1.wrongFeedback: Large deflections (bouncing back) need a large force. Only a packed, dense positive charge can give that. This showed the nucleus is tiny, holds all the positive charge and most of the mass.

2.question: An atom has an atomic number of 8 and a mass number of 18. How many neutrons does it have?
2.correctFeedback: Correct! Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 18 − 8 = 10.
2.wrongFeedback: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 18 − 8 = 10. The atomic number counts protons only. Subtract it from the mass number to find neutrons.

3.question: An electron absorbs electromagnetic radiation. What happens to it?
options: It moves to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus
It moves to a lower energy level, closer to the nucleus
3.correctFeedback: Correct! Absorbing radiation gives the electron energy. It moves to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus.
3.wrongFeedback: Absorbing radiation gives the electron energy. So it moves to a higher energy level, further from the nucleus. Emitting radiation moves it back down.

commonMistakes: Saying 'the atom is mostly empty space' without linking it to the Rutherford experiment. Link it to the fact that most alpha particles went straight through.
Mixing up mass number and atomic number. Atomic number is protons only (bottom number). Mass number is protons + neutrons (top number).
Saying electrons are 'in the nucleus'. They are outside it, at set distances called energy levels. Only protons and neutrons are in the nucleus.
Describing Rutherford's experiment as 'light fired at gold'. It used alpha particles (positively charged helium nuclei), not light.
Forgetting that a neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons. That number equals the atomic number.
examTips: For the alpha particle scattering experiment, always give three separate observations. Match each one to a conclusion about structure. Usually there is one mark per observation and conclusion pair.
To find the number of neutrons: neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Write this formula down before calculating.
Compare the plum pudding model and the nuclear model. The key difference is where the positive charge is. It is spread out in one, and packed into a tiny nucleus in the other.
If asked why the plum pudding model was dropped, say what it failed to predict. It did not predict the large-angle deflections and backscattering of alpha particles.

Atom radius about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Nucleus radius less than 1/10 000 of that
Proton: +1 charge, mass 1. In the nucleus
Neutron: 0 charge, mass 1. In the nucleus
Electron: −1 charge, very small mass. Outside the nucleus
Atomic number (Z) = proton number = electron number (neutral atom)
